how-much-to-charge-for-drone-mapping.htm.text:
← Drone Mapping Job Calculator

How much should you charge for drone mapping?

The honest answer is that price per acre is not a price, and the reason is specific rather than philosophical: the term that moves a mapping job most does not appear in a per-acre quote at all. That term is overlap. This page prices one real job all the way through so you can see where the money actually goes, and then changes exactly one input to show the problem.

Price your own job →

The job

100 acres of a construction site, flown on a DJI Mavic 3E at 120 m AGL, 75% front and 70% side overlap, 10 m/s, five ground control points, an hour of round-trip travel and 45 miles of it. Field rate $125/hr, processing $95/hr, mileage $0.70, target margin 40%. Every figure below comes out of the calculator on this site with those inputs.

1. Resolution first, because it sets everything else

Start at the deliverable, not the parcel. The client's required ground sample distance decides your altitude, and altitude decides the footprint, the line count, the image count and the processing bill. The formula is: 

GSD (cm/px) = sensor width (mm) × altitude (m) × 100
              ────────────────────────────────────────
              focal length (mm) × image width (px)

The Mavic 3E has a 17.3 mm wide sensor, a true focal length of 12.29 mm, and a 5280 px wide frame. At 120 m that is 3.20 cm/px. Use the “35 mm equivalent” focal length here with the real sensor width and you get a plausible-looking number and a flight that comes back at the wrong resolution — it is the most common error in a hand-rolled mapping spreadsheet, and it fails silently.

2. Footprint becomes flight lines

At 3.20 cm/px a 5280 × 3956 frame covers 169 × 127 m of ground. Overlap is what is left over:

  • Side overlap 70% → lines are 50.7 m apart (169 × 0.30)
  • Front overlap 75% → an exposure every 31.6 m (127 × 0.25)

100 acres is 404,686 m², so a square site is 636 m on a side. That gives 13 flight lines of 22 exposures each — 286 images over 8.9 km of path.

A note on the square: acreage alone does not determine a flight, and a square is the shape with the least perimeter for a given area. So this is the optimistic end of the range. Real parcels run longer, never shorter. For a corridor — a pipeline, a road, a transmission line — price from length and swath width instead, because the square model will be badly wrong.

3. Airtime is a small part of the day

8.9 km at 10 m/s is 14.8 minutes, plus 8 seconds of turn overhead on each of 12 turns: 16.4 minutes in the air. One sortie, no battery swap.

And here is the first thing worth noticing about mapping economics:

Where the 136 billable field minutes go.
ActivityMinutesShare
Travel, round trip6044%
Setup and site walk3022%
Ground control, 5 × 6 min3022%
Actually flying16.412%

Airtime is 12% of the field time. A pilot who prices “the flight” has priced an eighth of the job, and a pilot who discounts because “it is only a twenty-minute flight” has discounted against a number that was never the cost.

4. Processing follows the image count

286 images at 9 seconds each of attended time is 43 minutes. Set that rate from your own machine and your own workflow — it is the input people guess at most, and it is worth timing once against a job you have already delivered.

This is the line that a per-acre quote cannot see, which is the whole problem, and section 6 is where it bites.

5. The quote

LineBasisAmount
Field time136 min @ $125/hr$284.16
Processing43 min @ $95/hr$67.93
Mileage45 mi @ $0.70$31.50
Total cost$383.58
Price at 40% margincost ÷ 0.6$639.31

That is $6.39 per acre, and $255.72 of margin.

Margin is not markup. A 40% margin means price = cost ÷ 0.6. Adding 40% to cost gives cost × 1.4 = $537.02, which is a 28.6% margin, not 40%. On a job with $1,000 of cost the two answers are $1,666.67 and $1,400.00 — a $267 difference on one sortie, repeated on every job you ever quote. This is the single most common arithmetic error in trade pricing and it always runs in the same direction.

6. Now change one number

The client asks for “a bit more overlap — say 80/80”. Same site, same aircraft, same altitude, same rates:

OverlapImagesAirtimeCostPrice
70 / 7023416.4 min$371.23$618.72
80 / 8051323.6 min$452.42$754.03

2.19× the images. 1.44× the airtime. $135.30 more to quote — 21.9% on a job whose acreage did not change by a single square foot.

Why the two ratios differ is the mechanism worth internalising:

  • Image count goes as 1 / ((1−front) × (1−side)). At 70/70 you keep 30% of each: 1 / (0.3 × 0.3) = 11.1. At 80/80 you keep 20%: 1 / (0.2 × 0.2) = 25.0. That ratio is 2.25 — a quadratic, not a linear, response to a number people discuss in linear terms.
  • Airtime goes only as 1 / (1−side), because only side overlap adds flight lines. Front overlap just triggers the shutter more often along a line you were flying anyway. 3.33 → 5.0, about 1.5×.

So the flight looks nearly the same and the processing more than doubles. If you quoted per acre, you absorbed all of it.

7. The one the regulation decides

Resolution does not run upward without limit. 14 CFR 107.51(b) caps a small unmanned aircraft at 400 ft AGL — 121.92 m — unless you are within 400 ft of a structure or hold a waiver. If a coarse target GSD would need more altitude than that, you cannot simply climb: you fly at the ceiling, deliver a finer GSD than was asked for, and cover less ground per pass, so the job takes longer than an unrestricted plan implies. The calculator flags that case rather than quietly planning an altitude you cannot legally fly.

What to do with this

  1. Quote the specification, not the acreage. Put GSD and overlap on the quote as named terms. A change to either is a change order.
  2. Time your own processing once. Seconds-per-image is the input most often guessed and it scales with the term that moves most.
  3. Bill travel and ground control explicitly. They were 66% of the field time here and they are invisible in a per-acre number.
  4. Check the battery count against the sortie count before you commit to a date. A short day is a second mobilisation.

Open the calculator →

Worked example, not a rate card. Every figure here comes from the inputs named at the top of this page. Your rates, your aircraft, your processing workflow and your market are different, and the point of the calculator is to put your own numbers through the same arithmetic rather than to adopt these.

FOR PART 107 PILOTS QUOTING AERIAL MAPPING AND SURVEY WORK

Overlap is not a ten percent decision.

Going from 70/70 to 80/80 sounds like a small concession to make on a call. It is 2.25× the photographs — because image count goes as 1 / ((1−front) × (1−side)), not as the overlap itself. Airtime barely moves, about 1.5×, since only side overlap adds flight lines. So the flight looks almost the same and the processing bill more than doubles, and a pilot quoting by the acre pays that difference personally.

Put your own job in. Everything runs in this browser; nothing is uploaded.

Compare: this calculator vs. DroneDeploy, or this calculator vs. a flat per-acre quote.

1. The site and the camera

Area drives everything downstream. The plan assumes a square site — the least-perimeter shape, so treat the airtime as a floor rather than a midpoint.

2. The flight

Altitude sets resolution. The 400 ft (121.92 m) Part 107 ceiling is checked against what your target resolution would need.

3. Time and money

Margin is taken on the price, not added to cost — a 40% margin is cost / 0.6, not cost × 1.4.

Common questions

How do you calculate ground sample distance for a drone survey?

GSD in centimetres per pixel is the physical sensor width in millimetres, times altitude in metres, times 100, divided by the true focal length in millimetres times the image width in pixels. The 100 converts metres to centimetres, and the two millimetre figures cancel, which is why the formula needs a physical sensor width rather than a crop factor. The mistake that quietly ruins a spreadsheet is using the 35 mm equivalent focal length alongside the real sensor width: the answer still looks plausible and the flight comes back at the wrong resolution.

Why does raising overlap from 70% to 80% cost so much more than it sounds?

Because image count scales as one divided by the product of the two remaining fractions. At 70% front and 70% side you keep 30% of each, so the count goes as 1 / (0.3 x 0.3). At 80/80 you keep 20% of each, so it goes as 1 / (0.2 x 0.2). That is 2.25 times the photographs for what sounds like ten more percent. Airtime rises much less, around 1.5 times, because only side overlap adds flight lines — front overlap just triggers the shutter more often along a line you were already flying. So the airtime barely moves, the image count more than doubles, and the processing bill follows the image count. A pilot quoting by the acre absorbs that difference personally.

Does a finer GSD mean a longer flight?

Yes, and roughly as the square. A finer GSD needs a lower altitude, a lower altitude gives a smaller ground footprint per frame, and a smaller footprint means both more flight lines across the site and more exposures along each one. Halving the GSD halves the altitude, which halves the footprint in both directions and so roughly quadruples the image count and doubles the number of lines. Agreeing a resolution on a call without pricing it again is one of the more expensive habits in this trade.

Can I fly high enough to get any GSD I want?

No. 14 CFR 107.51(b) caps a small unmanned aircraft at 400 feet above ground level, which is 121.92 metres, unless you are within 400 feet of a structure or hold a waiver. If a coarse target GSD would need more altitude than that, you fly at the ceiling instead, get a finer GSD than the client asked for, and cover less ground per pass — so the flight takes longer than an unrestricted plan suggests. This calculator flags that case rather than quietly planning an illegal altitude. It does not grant any authorisation, check airspace, or file anything: LAANC, airspace class and currency remain entirely yours.

What does this assume about the shape of the site?

That it is square. Acreage alone does not determine a flight — a long thin corridor and a square block of the same area fly very differently — and a square is the shape with the least perimeter for a given area. That makes this the optimistic end of the range rather than a neutral guess, so real flights over awkward parcels run longer, not shorter. Treat the airtime as a floor. For a corridor job, price it from the corridor length and swath width instead of from acreage.

Is margin the same as markup?

No, and confusing them is how a job that looked profitable is not. Margin is a share of the price: a 40% margin means price equals cost divided by 0.6. Markup is a share of the cost: adding 40% to cost gives price equals cost times 1.4, which is only a 28.6% margin. On a $1,000 job the margin figure quotes $1,667 and the markup figure quotes $1,400 — a $267 difference on one sortie, repeated on every job. This calculator takes margin on the price, which is what pilots mean when they say it.

Is any of this uploaded?

No. There is no account and the page makes no network requests — it runs entirely in your browser. Your site areas, your hourly rates, the margin you quote at and the jobs you price are never sent anywhere and never appear in a usage count. The optional counter records only which features were used and the day, stored on your own device, and it switches itself off for browsers sending Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control.

Is this a flight plan, and can I fly from it?

No to both. It is a worksheet: arithmetic on figures you type. It is not a flight plan, not an airspace authorisation, and not aviation, legal or safety advice. It does not know your terrain, your obstacles, your airspace, the weather, your battery health or your aircraft's real endurance, and every one of those changes the flight it describes. Plan the actual mission in your ground control software, check airspace and obtain any authorisation you need, and treat these numbers as an estimate to quote from rather than a mission to fly.

vs-a-flat-per-acre-quote.html.text:
← Drone Mapping Job Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat per-acre quote

“$X an acre” is not a price for a mapping flight — it is a price for one specific overlap setting, altitude, and camera, quietly applied to every site that calls in, however that site is actually going to be flown.

What a flat per-acre rate is

A flat per-acre rate is the fastest way to quote aerial mapping work: multiply the site's acreage by a number and read off a price. It is the number a client holding a competitor's quote will ask you to match, whatever overlap or resolution the job actually needs.

The number behind it was set for one flight — one overlap setting, one altitude, one camera — and then reused for every site afterward, whether or not the next job is flown anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter your camera's sensor width, true focal length and image dimensions, the site area, altitude, front and side overlap, ground speed, battery window, and your field and processing rates. It computes ground sample distance, flight-line spacing, image count, airtime, sorties, and processing hours from those terms directly, then prices the job at your target margin — for this flight, not a generic one.

What a flat per-acre rate doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/acre at 70/70 overlap and 80/80 overlap on the identical site, even though 80/80 is 2.19x the images to capture and process. Prices image count, flight lines, and processing hours directly from the overlap you enter, so a higher-overlap flight of the same site costs more.
Has no line for altitude or ground sample distance, regardless of whether the client asked for a coarse GSD or a fine one. Computes GSD from sensor width, focal length, and altitude, and flags a target GSD that would need more altitude than the 400 ft Part 107 ceiling allows.
Has no line for battery swaps, ground control points, or the processing time that follows image count. Prices sorties, battery swaps, ground control, and processing hours separately, so a longer or more image-heavy flight costs more than a short one.
Gives the pilot a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the price at your target margin and the dollar gap against a flat per-acre rate, so a shopped price can be scored before you commit to it.

The same 100 acres, the same flat rate

Using this calculator's own shipped example (Mavic 3E, 120 m altitude, 40% target margin, the same field and processing rates throughout):

FlightImagesThis calculator's priceThe flat $6.19/acre rateGap
100 acres at 70/70 overlap — the flight the rate is set from234$618.72 ($6.19/acre)$618.72 (exactly $6.19/acre — this rate is fit to this flight)No gap on the flight the rate was built on.
The identical 100-acre site, flown at 80/80 overlap513 (2.19×)$754.03 at the same 40% margin$618.72 — acreage did not change, so the flat rate does not eitherThe flat rate is $135.30 short. Quoted at it anyway, the realized margin on this flight falls from 40% to about 26.9%.

The $6.19/acre rate is not invented — it is this calculator's own price on the 70/70 flight, divided by that flight's acreage. It fits that one flight by construction. Applied to the identical site flown at 80/80, it never sees that overlap moved at all, because acreage — the only input a per-acre rate reads — stayed at 100 either way. Run your own site and overlap settings in the calculator to see where they fall.

A flat per-acre rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one flight it was built for, and nothing about a per-acre number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not know your local market; it replaces the arithmetic a per-acre rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat per-acre rate get a drone mapping quote wrong?

Because the cost driver most of the time is the overlap specification, not acreage. Image count goes as 1/((1-front)x(1-side)), so going from 70/70 to 80/80 overlap on the exact same site is 2.19x the images to fly and process -- a job whose footprint did not change at all. A per-acre rate has no line for overlap, so it charges a 70/70 flight and an 80/80 flight of the same site identically.

What does a per-acre rate usually leave out entirely?

Front and side overlap, ground sample distance, and the processing time that follows image count. A finer GSD needs a lower altitude, a lower altitude means a smaller footprint per frame, and a smaller footprint means more flight lines and more exposures -- all before acreage enters the arithmetic at all. Acreage says nothing about which resolution or overlap a given job was agreed to.

How big is the gap in practice?

On this calculator's own 100-acre worked example (Mavic 3E at 120 m, 40% target margin): a 70/70 flight prices at $618.72 -- $6.19 an acre. Setting a per-acre rate from that job and applying it to the identical 100-acre site flown at 80/80 still quotes $618.72, because acreage did not change. The 80/80 flight's own price at the same 40% margin is $754.03, so the flat rate is $135.30 short. Quoted at the flat rate, the realized margin on the 80/80 job falls from the intended 40% to about 26.9% -- more than 13 points of margin given up on a job that looked identical on paper.

Is a flat per-acre rate ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs -- same overlap, same altitude, same camera, similar site shape -- a per-acre rate can land close, because none of the terms that actually move cost are varying. The risk is applying the same rate outside that band without noticing, because the rate does not know which overlap or altitude a new job was agreed to and neither does the pilot until the flight is actually planned.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local field or processing rates. It takes your camera's sensor geometry, the site area, altitude, overlap settings, and your own hourly rates, and turns that into ground sample distance, image count, airtime, and a price at your target margin -- the arithmetic a flat per-acre rate skips, not a market survey.

vs-dronedeploy.html.text:
← Drone Mapping Job Calculator

This calculator vs. DroneDeploy

Two different shapes: DroneDeploy is an account-based cloud platform for flying, processing and sharing aerial maps and 3D models. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this mapping job cost, given its overlap, altitude, site size and processing time — before you ever open a flight-planning app.

What each tool is for

DroneDeploy is a cloud reality-capture platform used by mapping and survey pilots, agronomists, construction and mining teams to plan and fly an automated mission from a mobile app, upload the captured images, process them into orthomosaics, point clouds, 3D models and other survey outputs, and share and measure the results with a team or client, tied to one account used on an ongoing paid basis across every flight a company runs. DroneDeploy's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page. Public descriptions of that flight-planning and cloud-processing platform describe capturing and turning images into maps and models once a mission is flown; none describe working out what a mapping job should cost, in dollars, from its ground sample distance, overlap settings, flight-line count, battery swaps and processing time — which is the one thing this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what DroneDeploy does. It does not fly a mission, capture an image, stitch an orthomosaic, or store a project in an account. It takes one job's sensor width and true focal length, site area, altitude, front and side overlap, ground speed, usable battery window and batteries carried, and turns that into ground sample distance, flight-line spacing, exposure spacing, image count, path length, airtime, sorties and battery swaps — then adds setup, ground-control-point time, battery swap time and travel, prices field and processing hours separately, and turns the total into the price that clears a target margin taken on price rather than as a markup on cost, plus a side-by-side of the same site at four overlap settings. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it

Would my target GSD need more altitude than the 400 ft Part 107 ceiling allows?This calculator's Part 107 ceiling check.
I already fly through DroneDeploy and need cloud processing, storage and client-facing maps across many projects.DroneDeploy — built as an ongoing, account-based platform for exactly that job.
How does the math behind a drone mapping bid actually work?This calculator's own worked example.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. DroneDeploy's tools are used through a paid account.

Most mapping pilots get different value from each: DroneDeploy (or a comparable reality-capture platform) for flying, processing and sharing maps as an ongoing account, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login answer to what one mapping job should cost from its overlap, altitude and site size before a flight-planning app is ever opened. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a captured image, a processed map, or a stored project.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or DroneDeploy?

They do different jobs, and a mapping pilot of any size will likely end up touching both. DroneDeploy is a cloud reality-capture platform used to plan and fly an automated mapping mission from a mobile app, upload the resulting images, process them into orthomosaics, 3D models and other survey outputs, and share and measure the results with a team or client, tied to one account used on an ongoing paid basis across a company's flights. DroneDeploy's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here, and no dollar figure for it appears anywhere on this page. This calculator does one narrower thing: starting from your camera's physical sensor width and true focal length, the site area, altitude, front and side overlap and ground speed, it computes ground sample distance, flight-line spacing, exposure spacing, image count, path length and airtime; adds sorties, battery swaps, setup, ground-control and travel time; adds the processing hours that follow the image count; and turns that into total cost and the price that clears a target margin taken on price, before any image is ever captured or a flight-planning app is opened. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A pilot who already flies through DroneDeploy and wants a cloud pipeline for capture, processing and client-facing maps is better served there; a pilot who wants an instant, private answer to what a mapping job should cost from its overlap, altitude and site size before ever opening a flight app is in the right place here.
